chapters.summary: Calvin Brown, Deputy Commissioner for Neighborhood Development at SBS, testifies in support of Intro 1112-A. He explains SBS oversees 78 BIDs and requires board approval, written justification, and Council support letters before assessment increases reach the Council.
chapters.title: Calvin Brown introduces SBS role in overseeing BID assessment increases

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: I'm Chair Lee and members of the Finance Committee.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: My name is Calvin Brown.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Neighborhood Development at the Department of Small Business Services, and I'm here to testify in support of Intro 112, a bill that would authorize an increase in the amount to be expended in eight business improvement districts.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Part of the role in overseeing and support in the city's existing network of 78 bids includes guiding them through various legislative processes, such as increases to the assessment caps and changes to the district plans.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: To propose an assessment increase, bids must complete a multi-step review process overseen by SBS.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: The bid board of directors, which includes local property owners, merchants, residents, as well as representatives from the city controller, borough president, city council, and SBS must review and approve the proposed change.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: SBS requires all...

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: bids to submit an in-depth written justification, proof of board approval, and letters of support from an overlapping or overlapping city council members.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: SBS then reviews these justifications and determines whether they are sufficient to be brought before city council.

chapters.summary: Brown says each BID published notice of the hearing in a local newspaper, specifying the time, place, and proposed assessment change. SBS confirmed the notices were completed at least 10 days before the hearing.
chapters.title: Brown details public notice and timing requirements for BID assessment increases

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: As required by law, each bid published a notice of today's public hearing at least once in a local newspaper having general circulation in the district specifying the time and the place of today's hearing and stating a change to their assessment amount.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: SBS collected record of these notices and confirms they were completed on time at least 10 days before today's hearing.

chapters.summary: Brown says SBS prioritizes assessment increases that enhance district programs and services. The increases will support supplemental sanitation and public safety services affected by inflation and minimum wage increases, and they vary by budget and district size.
chapters.title: Brown says BID increases will fund core services, sanitation, and public safety

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: It is SBS priority that assessment increase proposals focus on enhancing programs and services provided to the district.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Each bid proposing an assessment increase today is doing so to address vital needs and changing conditions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: The increases will further expand, reinforce, and strengthen core services currently provided in the business districts.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: This may include funds for strengthening current services, creating new and expanding programming, and or added staff capacity.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Additionally, portions of these increases will be used to sustain or increase current levels of supplemental sanitation,

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: public safety services that are impacted by the rising costs related to inflation and minimum wage increases.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: The proposed increases vary according to budget size, district size, and proposed changes in program and services.

chapters.summary: Brown enumerates the eight proposed increases: Queens 82nd Street and Greater JFK; Manhattan 34th Street, East Mid-Manhattan, and West Village; Bronx Southern Boulevard; and Brooklyn Bay Ridge Fifth Avenue and Myrtle Avenue Brooklyn. He provides the current and proposed dollar amounts for each.
chapters.title: Brown lists proposed BID assessment increases by borough

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: The proposed increases are Queens, 82nd Street bid from $254,450 to $304,500.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Greater JFK bid from 500,000 to 800,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: In Manhattan, 34th Street bid from 14,300,000 to 16,300,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: East Mid-Manhattan bid from 3,500,000 to 6,000,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: West Village bid, $594,906 to $1,400,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: The Bronx Southern Boulevard bid from $200,000 to $600,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: And in Brooklyn, Bay Ridge Fifth Avenue bid from $534,000 to $600,000.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: And Myrtle Avenue Brooklyn bid from $575,000 to $775,000.

chapters.summary: Brown says most BIDs will phase in increases over several years to minimize impact on property owners. Each year, BID boards will vote on how much to bill starting in FY28, and representatives from each named BID are present to answer specific questions.
chapters.title: Brown explains multi-year phase-in and annual board votes for BID increases

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Most of these bids will phase in increases over several years to minimize the impact on property owners in their district.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Each year, the bid board of directors will vote on how much to bill for the upcoming fiscal year starting in FY28.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: Representatives from each of the bid named in the law are present to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: pertaining to specific requests.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: And however, I'm happy to answer any general questions that you all may have.

chapters.summary: Mealy asks why Brooklyn BIDs are not seeking increases up to $1 million, wondering whether they are not applying or their needs are smaller. Brown says it depends on the BID board's appetite and what property owners feel comfortable paying.
chapters.title: Council Member Mealy asks Brown about Brooklyn BID funding disparity

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask, what's the disparity?

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Brooklyn, it's like it's not Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: All the bids is not up to a million.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Is that because they.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: not applying or their need is not big enough to get to a million dollars?

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: No, we do have some bids in Brooklyn that have budgets that are of a million.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: It's really based on the appetite because these increases have to go before the board of directors.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: So when they're proposing these increases, they engage the board of directors around what they feel comfortable paying additionally.

utterances.speaker: Calvin Brown
utterances.text: So it's really up to the property owners, the board of directors that sit on these bids.

utterances.speaker: Darlene Mealy
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Lee opens public testimony on Intro 1112-A. She states decorum rules, limits speakers to two minutes, prohibits video and audio recordings, and explains how to submit written testimony to the Sergeant at Arms or by email within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Chair Lee opens public testimony and outlines two-minute rule

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, and now we are going to...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So before we begin, I want to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify on proposed intro 11128 only.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And no video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms, and we'd...

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: your name to be called.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Once you have been recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on proposed intro 1112A.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms, and you may also email written testimony to

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Testimony at council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And the committee staff listen to and read every single word of your written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So if you have not, if folks have not submitted, please do so.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: When you hear your name, please come up to the witness panel, and I will now call.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Do we have any?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee

chapters.summary: Susan Peters, a frequent speaker, testifies that private commercial banks create the money supply as debt and collect interest as profit. She submits a printout and presentation, urges Council members to research the monetary system, and links it to the affordability crisis.
chapters.title: Susan Peters testifies on private commercial banks creating money as debt

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Let me just get my papers out here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Oh, here it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: How many minutes do I get?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I come every month to speak to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: My name is Susan Peters, a resident of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I wish to testify to this committee about the need of the council members to understand more clearly the monetary system we all depend on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: People think of it

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: as the Federal Reserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I call it the monetary system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: The monetary system is a system that creates the money we all need for to pay our bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: When the council speaks about the affordability crisis, you are talking about the lack of money in citizens'hands

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: to pay for the goods and services to live a decent life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Some entity has to create the money, so there exists money that people can earn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Most people think the money comes from our government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I include for the counselors a printout of a presentation proving that private commercial banks create our money as debt to borrowers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: on which these private commercial banks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: On which these private commercial banks are taking interest as profit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Hard to believe our money supply is created by private commercial banks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: The laws have allowed this and without public scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: You and the American people are kept in the dark.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: And I include here, and I have copies for everybody here and here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: It's a presentation, recent presentation, of someone who has studied the laws on banking and money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: And he proves how governments turn commercial bank debt into money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Our money is privately created and earning interest for private entities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: This is our money supply, our entire money supply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: It's kept secret because it's not talked about in the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: It's not talked about in schools of economics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: I'm telling you to do your own research and do good by the American public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Susan Peters
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: Committee on Finance held a hearing on Intro 1112-A, which would authorize assessment increases for eight business improvement districts.
The committee voted on a transparency resolution and three Article 11 real property tax exemption resolutions, adopting the coupled items.
SBS Deputy Commissioner Calvin Brown testified on BID review and proposed increases; public testimony included Kyle Ems on hearing scope and Susan Peters on the monetary system.
title: Committee on Finance
topic: Authorizing an increase in the amount to be expended annually in eight business improvement districts
